title: Two-Sample Intervals and Tests
short: Compare two proportions or two means.
trouble: Students treat paired data as two independent samples.

blocks.html: Most real questions compare two groups: a new drug against a placebo, one school against another, before against after. Two-sample methods combine the one-sample t procedures with the rule that variances of independent quantities add. But first you must decide whether the data are two independent samples or pairs.

Independent samples: for means, $$SE = \sqrt{\dfrac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \dfrac{s_2^2}{n_2}}, \quad t = \dfrac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{SE}$$ (df from software, or conservatively the smaller $n - 1$). For proportions, $$SE = \sqrt{\hat{p}_1(1 - \hat{p}_1)/n_1 + \hat{p}_2(1 - \hat{p}_2)/n_2}$$ for an interval; a test uses the pooled $\hat{p}$. Paired data (the same subjects twice, or matched pairs): take the differences and run a one-sample t procedure on them.

$\bar{x}_1$ and $\bar{x}_2$ come from independent samples, so the variance of their difference is the sum of their variances, $s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2$. In paired data the two measurements on one person are strongly related: a strong reader scores high both before and after. Taking differences cancels that person-to-person variation, leaving only the change, so the standard error is much smaller. Treating paired data as independent throws that advantage away.

blocks.title: Two independent groups
blocks.q: Group 1: $n_1 = 25$, $\bar{x}_1 = 78$, $s_1 = 10$. Group 2: $n_2 = 16$, $\bar{x}_2 = 70$, $s_2 = 12$. Find the standard error, t, and a 95% interval for $\mu_1 - \mu_2$ (conservative df $= 15$, $t^* = 2.131$).
steps: The interval is entirely above 0, consistent with a two-sided test rejecting "no difference" at the 0.05 level.

blocks.cap: Reading scores for 8 students before and after a summer program.

blocks.title: Paired data
blocks.q: Use the table to test whether scores rose. Compare with the (wrong) independent-samples analysis.
steps: Paired t: $SE = 1.51/\sqrt{8} \approx 0.53$, so $t = 3/0.53 \approx 5.61$ with 7 df: a p-value well below 0.01.
Treated as independent: the SDs of the before and after scores are about 9.1 and 8.7, so $SE \approx 4.45$ and $t \approx 0.67$: no evidence at all.
The students differ a lot from each other, but each one improved a little. Only the paired analysis sees that.
blocks.a: Paired: t ≈ 5.6, strong evidence; independent (wrong): t ≈ 0.7.

blocks.html: Treating paired data as two independent samples. When each value in one group is linked to one value in the other (same person, twins, matched plots), analyze the differences. Check: could you draw a line from each "before" value to its own "after" value?

For two proportions, for example 60 of 200 against 45 of 200: $\hat{p}_1 = 0.30$, $\hat{p}_2 = 0.225$, and the pooled $\hat{p} = 105/400 = 0.2625$ gives $$SE = \sqrt{0.2625 \cdot 0.7375\,(1/200 + 1/200)} \approx 0.044$$ and $z \approx 1.70$ (two-sided p ≈ 0.09).
